advances:
Excludes Regime A Alternative 3 \(q=0<\omega\) throughout the exact
registered parameter strip. The proof first forces a sharp
\(8s/9\) lower bound on the sum of the two side middle caps, then
contradicts the exact small-endpoint identity
\(v_i+v_\ell=r+\omega\).
author: mp_r92_regime_a_residual_alternatives
proof:
We first record the planar centroid halfspace inequality in the form
needed below: if a closed halfplane contains the centroid of a planar
convex body of area \(s\), then its intersection with the body has area
at least \(4s/9\).

For completeness, rotate and translate so that the cutting line is
\(\{x=0\}\) and the centroid has first coordinate zero. The vertical
section length \(\varphi(x)\) is nonnegative and concave on its support,
and
\[
\int x\varphi(x)\,dx=0.
\]
The elementary one-dimensional concavity lemma says that each side of
zero has at least \(4/9\) of the total integral. One standard proof is
the one-dimensional localization argument: under fixed zeroth and first
moments, a minimizer of either side integral among nonnegative concave
functions is affine on its support. For an affine function with endpoint
values \(A,B\ge0\) on an interval of length one, its centroid is at
\[
\lambda=\frac{A+2B}{3(A+B)}
\]
from the left endpoint. Direct integration gives
\[
\frac{\int_\lambda^1(A+(B-A)x)\,dx}
{\int_0^1(A+(B-A)x)\,dx}
-\frac49
=
\frac{B^2(3A+B)}{9(A+B)^3}\ge0,
\]
\[
\frac{\int_0^\lambda(A+(B-A)x)\,dx}
{\int_0^1(A+(B-A)x)\,dx}
-\frac49
=
\frac{A^2(A+3B)}{9(A+B)^3}\ge0.
\]
The localization reduction follows by polygonal approximation: an
interior downward jump of the slope admits a sufficiently small
piecewise-affine perturbation with zero zeroth and first moments; one
sign preserves concavity and decreases the chosen side integral, while
the zero-objective case removes that jump. Iterating leaves an affine
function, and uniform approximation gives the general concave case.
This proves the stated centroid halfspace inequality.

The strip (3) implies
\[
s>1-r,\qquad s<1+r,\qquad 0<r<\frac13.
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, in the second line of (3), \(2-4r<1+r\) because \(r>1/5\).
Using (2) and (7),
\[
\frac{4s}{9}-(t-r)
=\frac{2s+7r-2}{9}
>\frac{5r}{9}>0,
\tag{8}
\]
\[
t-\frac{4s}{9}
=\frac{2(1+r-s)}9>0.
\tag{9}
\]
Also \(t<s\): by \(s>1-r\) and \(r<1/3\),
\[
7s>7(1-r)>2(1+r).
\tag{10}
\]
Equations (4) and (8) give
\[
c_j<\frac{4s}{9}.
\tag{11}
\]
If \(f_j(g)\le0\), then the \(j\)-cap is a closed halfplane section
containing \(g\), so the centroid halfspace inequality contradicts
(11). Hence
\[
f_j(g)>0.
\tag{12}
\]

Equation (1) and (12) imply
\[
f_i(g)+f_\ell(g)<-1.
\]
At least one of these two values is nonpositive. Interchange \(i,\ell\)
if necessary and assume
\[
f_i(g)\le0.
\tag{13}
\]
The centroid halfspace inequality gives
\[
c_i\ge\frac{4s}{9}.
\tag{14}
\]
The first inequality in (5) gives \(c_i<t\).

Define
\[
F(x)=2\sqrt{sx}-2x.
\]
On \([4s/9,s]\),
\[
F'(x)=\sqrt{\frac{s}{x}}-2\le-\frac12,
\]
so \(F\) is strictly decreasing there. A direct substitution of
\(t=2(1+r+s)/9\) gives
\[
4st-(3t-r)^2
=
\frac{
4(s-1+r)(s+1+2r)+r(8-9r)
}{9}>0
\tag{15}
\]
by (7). Since \(3t-r=(2+2s-r)/3>0\), equation (15) yields
\[
F(t)=2\sqrt{st}-2t>t-r>c_j.
\tag{16}
\]
Equations (10), (14), and \(c_i<t\) place \(c_i\) in
\([4s/9,t)\), and therefore
\[
F(c_i)>F(t)>c_j.
\tag{17}
\]

If \(f_\ell(g)\le0\), the centroid halfspace inequality gives
\[
c_\ell\ge\frac{4s}{9}\ge F(c_i),
\tag{18}
\]
where the last inequality uses the monotonicity of \(F\) and
\(F(4s/9)=4s/9\). If \(f_\ell(g)>0\), apply accepted theorem
`0688f679297c8baa` with
\[
(f_1,f_2,f_3)=(f_\ell,f_j,f_i).
\]
Its hypotheses hold by (1), (12), and the present case
\(f_\ell(g)>0\), so
\[
\max\{c_\ell,c_j\}\ge F(c_i).
\]
Equation (17) rules out \(c_j\) as the maximizing term, and again
\[
c_\ell\ge F(c_i).
\tag{19}
\]

The function
\[
x+F(x)=2\sqrt{sx}-x
\]
is increasing for \(0<x<s\), because its derivative is
\(\sqrt{s/x}-1>0\). Equations (10), (14), and (18)-(19) therefore give
\[
c_i+c_\ell
\ge c_i+F(c_i)
\ge\frac{4s}{9}+F\left(\frac{4s}{9}\right)
=\frac{8s}{9}.
\tag{20}
\]

Finally add the two strict inequalities in (5), use nonnegativity of
\(u_i,u_\ell\), and substitute (6):
\[
c_i+c_\ell+r+\omega<2t.
\]
Together with (20),
\[
r+\omega
<2t-\frac{8s}{9}
=\frac{4(1+r-s)}9
<\frac{8r}{9}
<r,
\tag{21}
\]
where the penultimate inequality is strict by \(s>1-r\). This is
impossible because \(\omega>0\). Thus Alternative 3 is excluded
throughout (3). No step assumes that any \(u_h\) or \(v_h\) is positive,
so the cap-empty and cap-full boundaries are included.
statement:
Assume the exact Regime A strip of accepted fact `ab2620c83e116de2`
and Alternative 3 of accepted fact `879a3c45b5f50670`. More explicitly,
let \(K\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a nonempty two-dimensional compact convex
body of area \(s\) and centroid \(g\). Let \(f_i,f_j,f_\ell\) be
nonconstant affine functions with pairwise nonparallel linear parts and
\[
f_i+f_j+f_\ell=-1.
\tag{1}
\]
Put
\[
c_h=\left|K\cap\{f_h\le0\}\right|
\qquad(h=i,j,\ell),
\qquad
t=\frac{2(1+r+s)}9.
\tag{2}
\]
Assume
\[
\begin{cases}
0<r\le1/5,\quad 1-r<s<1+r,\\
\text{or}\\
1/5<r<1/3,\quad 1-r<s<2-4r,
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]
\[
c_j+r<t,
\tag{4}
\]
and that there are nonnegative \(u_i,u_\ell,v_i,v_\ell\) and
\(\omega>0\) such that
\[
c_i+u_i+v_i<t,\qquad
c_\ell+u_\ell+v_\ell<t,
\tag{5}
\]
\[
v_i+v_\ell=r+\omega.
\tag{6}
\]
Then these hypotheses are inconsistent. Consequently Alternative 3
\(q=0<\omega\) cannot occur anywhere in the full Regime A strip,
including \(r=1/5\) and all cap-empty or cap-full boundary cases.
